1.pericope_label: Jesus goes through the corn on the sabbath, and his disciples pluck the ears and eat

schools.summary: Gill supposes them on the way to worship; Calvin charges the Pharisees with the hypocrite’s habit of exactness in trifles and liberty in weighty things, moved more by envy than superstition.
Henry finds them erring by strictness where they usually erred by looseness, ritual zeal standing in for morals.

Robertson denies that the opening phrase fixes any time; Ellicott despairs of a harmony and locates the offence in reaping and threshing; Lightfoot reconstructs the Passover calendar behind the second-first sabbath; Barnes adds the season of the barley harvest.
Clarke reproduces the rabbinic reckoning of the sabbath almost verbatim; Wesley notes they took only what present necessity required.
Chrysostom grants that Christ meant to break the sabbath, but not absolutely and never without a sufficient reason, and admires disciples who would not leave him even under hunger.

The Gloss dates the scene after John’s death; Augustine weighs order of time against order of recollection, notes that the charge was sabbath-breaking and not theft, and reads the two examples as royal and priestly; Jerome supplies the crowding that left them unfed and the priest who preferred saving men to sacrifice; Hilary allegorises field, sabbath, corn and hunger; Raban makes the plucking and rubbing the work of those who search the Scriptures; Remigius takes the title Son of man as a claim to have made the law.

debates.question: Does at that time fix the occasion?

sides.position: It marks the year after John’s death
Perhaps the true order of time, perhaps merely indefinite
A definite word for a time we cannot fix
The harmonies differ so widely that the phrase belongs elsewhere
The second-first sabbath fixes it between Passover and Pentecost
Yes, deliberately, but never without a sufficient cause shown
Only the Pharisees’ reading of it, which counted plucking as reaping
Not at all; the fault lay in a superstition exact about trifles

2.pericope_label: The Pharisees charge the disciples with what is not lawful, and Christ answers with what David did

schools.summary: Calvin counts five arguments in the reply and insists that David was free from blame, since an unlawful act could not have served as a precedent; Gill turns the question back on men unfit to teach or censure if they had not read the Scriptures.

Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic law of the thirty-nine works that made plucking a kind of reaping, and fills in the history at Nob from the Hebrew side; Robertson matches plucking to reaping and rubbing to threshing and notes that David did the very thing charged; Barnes rests the complaint wholly on the day and draws the principle that necessity suspends law; Ellicott places the accusers as watchers from Jerusalem and reads the appeal as an argument from the greater to the less.

Clarke measures the superstition by the wars in which Jews would not defend themselves on the sabbath, and reproduces Lightfoot’s rabbinic citations almost verbatim; Wesley grants that David transgressed the law in a higher instance and that necessity was his plea.

sides.position: No; he was blameless, or the example would prove nothing
Yes, and in a higher instance than the disciples’
The act passed uncondemned, proving that necessity does not bind

debates.question: Why is the case of David chosen?

sides.position: Because it meets the Pharisees on their strongest ground, from greater to less
Because they must have read it, and were unfit to censure if they had not
Because the rabbis themselves allowed anything but idolatry, adultery and murder to preserve life

4.pericope_label: David eating the shewbread, and the priests who profane the sabbath and are blameless

schools.summary: Gill locates the tabernacle at Nob and lists the servile works the priests performed; Calvin makes the argument prove that duties of piety never conflict, presses the comparison from the temple to the spiritual temple whose worshippers the disciples were serving, and cautions that the word profane is accommodated to the hearers rather than strictly accurate.

Barnes describes the shewbread and details what the sabbath sacrifices required, including fires the Law forbade the people; Ellicott counts the loaves and draws the principle that necessity involving the good of man overrides positive command; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic maxim that there is no sabbatism at all in the temple.
Wesley makes the twelve loaves the twelve tribes; Clarke gives the Hebrew name and glosses profane as putting the day to common use.

debates.question: What does the priests’ example establish?

sides.position: That duties of piety never conflict, and that the spiritual temple sanctifies its servants the more
That men did in the temple what would have profaned the day elsewhere, and were blameless
That by the rabbis’ own maxim holy work is not servile and the temple keeps no sabbath

debates.question: Is profane the right word for what the priests did?

sides.position: Not strictly; it is accommodated to hearers who cannot judge properly
Yes, in the sense of putting the day to a common use

debates.q: Who or what is greater than the temple?

sides.a: Christ himself, a claim to deity
Something neuter: the body of the Son of Man as the true temple
Either Christ or the work and its servants

debates.q: How absolute is I will have mercy and not sacrifice?

sides.a: Comparative: rites are valued as directed to their object and are the lesser thing
A working rule: prefer mercy whenever the two interfere
One of four ways a positive law ceases to oblige

outliers: John Wesley suspects verses 7 and 8 have been transposed in the text

9.pericope_label: Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath

debates.q: Did this happen on the same sabbath as the cornfield?

sides.a: No: Luke says another sabbath, and Matthew leaves room for the interval
Matthew and Mark leave the impression of the same day, though they do not assert it

debates.q: Who put the question, the Pharisees or Jesus?

sides.a: Both, in sequence: they asked, he answered with a counter-question
The order matters less than the motive: they asked to accuse, not to learn

outliers: Raban reads the stretching out of the withered hand as a call to almsgiving

debates.q: Was the Pharisees’ question a genuine inquiry?

sides.a: No: the words of deniers, backed by canons against sabbath physic
No: a trap, with the accusation before the local court already resolved on
The question is malformed; they should have asked whose work it was

debates.q: What does the appeal to the sheep prove?

sides.a: An argument from the lesser to the greater that silenced them
That self-interest is a decisive casuist and dissolves their scruples
That withholding relief is itself sin, near neighbour to manslaughter

outliers: A.T. Robertson treats the verse only as a Hebraism in the interrogative particle

12.pericope_label: It is lawful to do well on the sabbath

debates.q: What kind of argument is the question about the man and the sheep?

sides.a: A proportion from the irrational creature to the rational
An argumentum ad hominem from their own maxims and conduct
An unanswered question that goes to the roots of things

debates.q: What does the command to a withered hand teach?

sides.a: Obey the command without first examining ability, but it proves nothing of the sinner’s power
Faith disregards apparent impossibilities; the effort to believe is the healing faith
The obedience itself proves the man had faith to be healed

outliers: Adam Clarke notes that a cure by word alone left the sabbath unbroken on the strictest reading

14.pericope_label: They took counsel to destroy him

debates.q: Why did Jesus withdraw?

sides.a: Not from fear, but to avoid aggravating their rage before the appointed hour
To take from the Pharisees every occasion of sin
Because a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem

debates.q: Who is the bruised reed and the smoking flax?

sides.a: The weak sinner and the little one whose spark of faith must not be despised
The Jews are the reed; the Gentiles the smoking flax raised to a flame
The reverse: the Gentiles are the reed, and the flax the Spirit not yet withdrawn from Israel
Both figure the persecutors, spared because he came to be judged and not to judge

outliers: Raban draws from the withdrawal a rule against seeking praise after a great work

15.pericope_label: He withdrew, and charged them not to make him known

debates.q: Why the charge not to make him known?

sides.a: To avoid the plots and save his life at this time
A general command: not yet the hour of conflict, so work while it is day
He would not be known by those who would not know him
Not repression but timing: let the report strike root and bear fruit in season

debates.q: What does the Isaiah citation establish?

sides.a: That the Messiah was predicted as retiring and peaceful, not as a conqueror
That power without ostentation marks the true ideal King
That divine glory is no less admirable under a veil of infirmity

outliers: A.T. Robertson notes that Matthew applies to Christ a prophecy often referred to Cyrus

18.pericope_label: Behold my servant whom I have chosen

debates.q: In what sense is the Messiah called servant?

sides.a: As mediator, employed and obedient in the work of salvation
From the humble condition and the form of a servant
As rendering the perfect service sinful man could not
Not of ordinary rank, but by eminence, as one called of God to the office

debates.q: What does judgment mean in the citation?

sides.a: Law, precepts, a whole body of doctrine: the gospel itself
The Hebrew allows mercy or justice; here the merciful gospel
Wide enough to include a king teaching righteousness, not only executing it

outliers: John Gill reads he shall not cry forensically, as Christ refusing the plaintiff’s part

20.pericope_label: A bruised reed shall he not break

debates.q: What are the bruised reed and the smoking flax?

sides.a: Measures of noise: Christ will make no more sound than a snapping reed or a hissing wick
The weak, the oppressed, the contrite soul and the languishing grace of believers
Reported but not adopted: the Jewish state, left to expire of itself
Interpreters vary and no reading is settled

debates.q: What is judgment unto victory?

sides.a: Christ breaking forth at last as judge and avenger on the nation that rejected him
The gospel prevailing, though not by the conquest the Jews expected
Compassion characterising the whole work until final judgment and truth prevail
A word implying combat: the kingdom is won only by fighting the devil

outliers: A.T. Robertson treats the verse chiefly as a note on a participle and a misplaced augment

22.pericope_label: The blind and dumb demoniac healed

debates.q: Is this the same event as the dumb demoniac of Matthew 9?

sides.a: Alike in cavil and answer, but not the same: that man was only dumb
The charge was probably repeated whenever the occasion arose
Luke omits the blindness but describes the same man, since the rest agrees

debates.q: Were the blindness and dumbness natural or demonic?

sides.a: Demonic: there was no defect in the optic nerves or the tongue
Demonic, and a warning about disorders now taken for natural
A deliberate blocking of the two inlets of faith, hearing and sight

outliers: Hilary alone reads the healed man as a figure of the salvation of the Gentiles rather than of the individual believer

23.pericope_label: Is not this the son of David?

debates.q: How much does the crowd’s question concede?

sides.a: Conviction, faith and confession
A sound inference from prophecy to the Messiah
The Greek expects the answer no; it is hesitation under hostile pressure
Not a full affirmation, but the thought that he might be the Christ

debates.q: What does the charge of Beelzebub concede?

sides.a: Superhuman power, which they could not deny, plus contempt for the worker
The reality of the healing, which forced them to assume demonic agency
Nothing willingly: an open fact turned into a reproach of magic

outliers: John Lightfoot derives the name from Zebul, a dunghill, rather than from the god of flies

debates.q: What follows from Christ answering their unspoken thought?

sides.a: It compelled them to reckon with one who sees the heart
It proves omniscience, and so deity and Messiahship
Knowing hearts belongs to God alone
It meets the rabbinic test that Messiah shall smell and judge

debates.q: Is the divided-kingdom argument conclusive?

sides.a: A dilemma with no third option
Conclusive from their own premises: Satan would show less than human prudence
Not quite satisfactory, since Satan can feign discord to entrap by superstition

outliers: Chrysostom notes that Christ withheld the accusers’ words to spare them, aiming to do the sinners good rather than publish their sin

26.pericope_label: By whom do your children cast them out?

debates.q: Who are your children?

sides.a: Disciples of the Pharisees who practised exorcism
The apostles, who were of that race and will judge from twelve thrones
The wording matters more than the referent: not my disciples, but yours

debates.q: Did those exorcists really cast out demons?

sides.a: No: the power was claimed, the practice magic or jugglery
No: a delusion, Satan feigning expulsion by compact with himself
Yes, and not by Beelzebub, or the question would not be valid

outliers: Jerome distinguishes three senses of the kingdom of God in this one verse

debates.q: What are the house and the goods?

sides.a: The region subject to Satan and the demons that maintain his dominion
This world, and all the unbelievers
The sinner’s own heart, surrendered of his own accord
The world divided among the apostles for conversion

debates.q: What does calling the adversary strong concede?

sides.a: His old reign, which arose out of our sloth; spoiling, not robbing, shows power
A reason not to be careless, since the conqueror himself calls him strong
That men cherish their slavery, so only a superior force can free them
That the plunder is itself the proof of the binding

outliers: Cyril of Jerusalem turns the verse against those who divide the lordship of soul and body between two gods

30.pericope_label: He that is not with me is against me

debates.q: Who is the one who is not with Christ?

sides.a: Satan, whose works are opposite at every point
The Jews, classed with the devil; or Christ speaking of himself
The scribes, doubly opposed because they intentionally hinder
Anyone at all: there are no neuters in this war

debates.q: How does this square with he that is not against us is for us?

sides.a: Different subjects: there a man on their side, here the devil
Opposite poles of one truth about neutrality

outliers: Adam Clarke could find no parallel to the scattering proverb in rabbinic, Greek or Roman writers

debates.q: What is the sin against the Spirit?

sides.a: Ascribing to the devil miracles wrought by the Spirit, and nothing else
The same, and these Pharisees had already committed it
A settled antagonism to goodness as good, which they were drifting toward
Not, as some define it, obstinacy persisted in until death

debates.q: Why is it graver than a word against the Son of man?

sides.a: Stumbling at the flesh is pardonable for the body’s little worth
Of the Spirit they could plead no ignorance, since the prophets spoke by him
It denies the substance of the Father’s Spirit in Christ
Not because the Spirit is greater than the Son

outliers: Gregory reads the clause as proof that lesser sins may be remitted in the world to come; the Gloss reads the same clause as destroying Origen’s universal pardon

32.pericope_label: Neither in this world, nor in the world to come

debates.q: What are this world and the world to come?

sides.a: A Jewish proverb for a thing that will never be done
The Jewish dispensation and the Christian
The age before the Christ and the age after, on whose boundary he stood
This life and the last judgment, with no middle state between

debates.q: Does the clause imply forgiveness after death?

sides.a: No: it echoes a rabbinic scale of expiations, not a doctrine of later pardon
No, and the contrary opinion is inconsistent with its own account of guilt
Yes: some sins wait for their full cancelling until the age to come

outliers: John Gill offers Saul the Pharisee as the standing case of a blasphemer against the Son of man forgiven

33.pericope_label: The tree is known by its fruit

debates.q: Is make the tree good a command or a test?

sides.a: The first half a precept of health, the second only a warning
Neither: make means reckon, a demand for logical consistency
A rhetorical form, not a grant of power over oneself
A rule of evidence they have inverted: the fruit proves the tree

debates.q: What does the reproach generation of vipers establish?

sides.a: Not anger, but a just declaration of character
That nothing else could be looked for from such a brood
That these men had deliberately taken Satan’s side
That hypocrisy colouring sin deserves a more terrible rebuke than other sins

outliers: Hilary reads the saying as convicting a later error, worshipping Christ as God while denying him the Father’s substance

debates.q: What is an idle word?

sides.a: A false word that accuses falsely
A word that does not edify; buffoonery is worse than idle
Literally useless, but here wicked and injurious, as the context requires
Deliberately not evil but purposeless, because random speech betrays character

debates.q: In what sense do words justify?

sides.a: Justified means acquitted, as men are also justified by faith and by works
Speech is not the ground; it only keeps a man from his own tongue’s condemnation
Only if the words proceed from the inmost heart and an entire purpose
Words are a chief part of the evidence, not the whole of it

outliers: John Gill notes that the closing sentence has been treated as a quotation though no such scripture exists

38.pericope_label: Master, we would see a sign

debates.q: What sign were they asking for?

sides.a: Something from the sky, beyond dispute: thunder, darkness, food rained down
Fire like Elijah’s, or thunder and rain out of season like Samuel’s
A warrant for the authority with which he had just spoken
Whatever they wanted, he gave one from the deep and kept the heavenly sign for the disciples

debates.q: Was the demand a fair one?

sides.a: Fair in principle, since miracles should prove a mission, but not after so many
Hypocrisy and irony from men who had just called him possessed
Pride and incredulity never have proof enough

outliers: Jerome raises against himself the objection that the magicians in Egypt also produced signs from the sky

39.pericope_label: The sign of the prophet Jonah

debates.q: How can three days and three nights cover two nights and part of three days?

sides.a: Eastern usage counts any part of a day as the whole
The silence of the Jews proves the reckoning was regular
It matches the rabbinic computation, as in the thirty-six hours of Joshua’s sun
Popular speech for three days, since he rose on the third and not the fourth

debates.q: What is the sign of Jonah?

sides.a: The burial and rising, not the preaching, which was no sign at all
The deliverance, believed by the Ninevites as the resurrection is to be believed
The whole resemblance, pressed detail by detail

outliers: John Calvin objects that God granted signs to Gideon and Hezekiah and blamed Ahaz for not asking one, so the fault cannot lie in the asking itself

41.pericope_label: The men of Nineveh and the queen of the south

debates.q: In what sense will they condemn this generation?

sides.a: Not by a sentence, but by the comparison of their example
By standing up as witnesses rather than by rising from the dead
By a single resurrection of good and bad, with judgment following at once

debates.q: Where did the queen of the south come from?

sides.a: Sheba in southern Arabia
Ethiopia, with Meroe on the Nile for its capital

outliers: Raban leaves the geography aside: the Ninevites figure those who cease from sin, the queen those who never learned it

debates.q: What are the dry places?

sides.a: Literal deserts, on the current belief that spirits haunt waterless regions
The hearts of the Gentiles, dry for want of Scripture and the Spirit
The opposite: the hearts of the faithful, dried of carnal lust so no footstep holds

debates.q: Who is the man in the parable?

sides.a: The Jewish people, and not heretics, as the closing words compel
The Jews, and ourselves too if we relapse after being enlightened
Believers who lack strength for continence and return to the world
Anyone outwardly reformed without the grace of God

outliers: Adam Clarke argues from the appeal itself that possession must have been real, since the scribes would have scorned an argument built on a vulgar error

45.pericope_label: The last state of that man

debates.q: What does the number seven mean here?

sides.a: A mocking allusion to the seven spirits before the throne, or simply completeness
A Jewish number for a thing filled up: as many as could occupy a soul
Intensity of possession rather than a count
Indefinite; and the comparative implies degrees among the devils

debates.q: What is the last state that is worse than the first?

sides.a: The return of unbelief after an outward reformation
A stage still future when Christ spoke, after idolatry had been expelled at the return from exile
The destruction that swept away the nation and its privileges
The doubled subjection of anyone who falls from grace, in any age

outliers: John Lightfoot doubts the usual reading, since no devil cast out by Christ ever returned, and takes the parable to allude to Jewish exorcists and their figments

46.pericope_label: His mother and his brethren stood without

debates.q: Who were the brethren of the Lord?

sides.a: Not sons of Mary: brother has four scriptural senses, and Scripture never names them hers
Children of his mother, the natural and obvious sense
Undecidable: no adequate evidence that the word was used of cousins as such

debates.q: Why did they call him out?

sides.a: Love of honour, and a claim of authority over him before the crowd
Concern: friends thought him beside himself, and his mother would take him home
They kept outside because his own received him not

outliers: Gregory makes a man Christ’s brother by believing and his mother by preaching, begetting the Lord in a hearer’s heart

47.pericope_label: Behold my mother and my brethren

debates.q: Why does the reply sound like a disregard of his mother?

sides.a: It is not: the question was a device to fix attention on the answer
They had come to seize him, thinking him distracted
It was a reproof: Mary acted improperly in interrupting his teaching
It states a principle: spiritual ties outrank natural ones where they clash

debates.q: What is it to do the will of the Father?

sides.a: Not perfect obedience to the law, but the obedience of faith to the Gospel
Inward fellowship: not the fact of baptism but what baptism signifies
Spiritual union, which puts any believer on a level with his nearest kin

outliers: A.T. Robertson notes that verse 47 is absent from the chief early manuscripts and was probably copied into Matthew from Mark or Luke
